[a7 1/2] # Village gets its first text-only library

Residents of Dunmore, a hill village with no mobile data signal, can now borrow the news by text message.

[a7 2/2] The scheme, run from the old post office, answers any question sent to a single number with a short, readable page - and it costs
>> p! a7 2

[a7 1/2] nothing to ask.

"People here have phones, they just don't have data," said Morag Keir[1], who started the project after the last bus route was

[a7 2/2] cut. She said the idea came from reading about the history of SMS[2] and the 160-character limit that shaped it.

## How it works
>> p! a7 3
[a7 1/2] A text is sent to the library's number. A computer in the post office fetches the answer, trims it to the words that matter and sends it back in a

[a7 2/2] handful of messages. Longer pages arrive in parts, and readers can ask for the next part whenever they like.
>> p! a7 4

[a7 1/2] - Search the web by texting a few words
- Open any page by texting its address
- Follow a link by texting its number

## What it costs

[a7 2/2] Each reply costs the library about six pence a message. The parish council has agreed to fund the first year, with a cap of two hundred
>> p! a7 5

[a7 1/2] messages a day.

1. A search usually takes four messages.
2. A news story usually takes twelve.
3. A long feature can take forty.

[a7 2/2] | Reply | Messages | Cost |
| Search | 4 | 24p |
| Story | 12 | 72p |

"It is slow, but it is ours," one reader wrote back.
>> p! a7 6
[a7 1/2] Questions about the scheme can go to the library or to the parish council[3]. Readers who want the large-print edition should ask at the counter. A
[a7 2/2] second, longer interview[1] with Morag Keir is on page four.
